newsitem.title: USA: Five indicted in U.S. software piracy scheme.
newsitem.headline: Five indicted in U.S. software piracy scheme.

text.p: A federal grand jury indicted five people and two businesses on charges of taking part in a multimillion-dollar software piracy scheme, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.

The case involved the largest-ever seizure of U.S.-produced counterfeit software, the U.S. Attorney's office for northern California said. Officials could not say how much the seized software was worth, however.

"Apart from the tremendous dollar value and quantity of software, what makes this case significant is that this operation occurred in Silicon Valley, the heart of the software publishing industry," said Leland Altschuler, Chief Assistant U.S. Attorney in San Jose.

The indictment alleged that between May 1992 and November 1993, Joe Huong, 34, James Sung, 49, Shirley Sung, 49, Michael Ma, 36, Anne Wang, 36, the U-Top Printing Co and the U-Win Printing Co took part in a conspiracy to manufacture copyrighted Microsoft Corp software and traffic in counterfeit goods.

Operating from San Jose and nearby Sunnyvale, the U-Top business was accused of reproducing and distributing more than 200,000 pirated copies of Microsoft Windows and MS-DOS 5.0 software, and selling more than $3 million worth of the illegally copied software, the U.S. Attorney's office said.

The 16-count indictment was handed up in San Jose in August 1995 but kept secret until now. The defendants faced various felony charges including criminal contempt, perjury, criminal infringement of copyright, trafficking in counterfeit goods and conspiracy to traffic in counterfeit goods.
Huong, of Taipei, Taiwan, was arrested by FBI and Customs agents at Los Angeles International Airport on Saturday while waiting to board a plane to Taiwan, Altschuler said.
Ma and Wang were expected to surrender before a U.S. magistrate in San Jose in the next two weeks, Altschuler said.
James and Shirley Sung were out of the United States and were believed to be in a country which did not have an extradition treaty with the United States, Altschuler said.
The criminal investigation began after Microsoft filed a civil lawsuit stemming from the U-Top operation in 1992, the U.S. Attorney's office said.
